title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
directAnswer: Combine a dynamic array (for O(1) random access by position) with a hash map value → index (for O(1) membership and lookup). insert appends and records the index. remove does the key trick: swap the target with the LAST array element, fix the moved element's index in the map, then pop the last slot — avoiding the O(n) shift. getRandom picks a uniformly random array index. All three are O(1) average.

remember.pattern: Array + value→index map, swap-with-last on delete
remember.formula:
remove(val):
    i = idx[val]; last = arr[-1]
    arr[i] = last; idx[last] = i   # move last into the hole
    arr.pop(); del idx[val]        # then drop the tail
rules: **Array gives O(1) getRandom**, hash map gives O(1) membership — you need *both*, neither alone suffices.
On remove, **swap the victim with the last element** then pop the tail; never delete from the middle (that's an O(n) shift).
After the swap, **update the moved element's index** in the map (`idx[last] = i`) — forgetting this is the #1 bug.
insert/remove return a **boolean** for whether the set changed; check membership first.
getRandom must be **uniform** — pick a random index into the array, which is contiguous, so every element is equally likely.
whenToUse: Need insert, delete, AND uniform random sample all in O(1)
A set-like structure that also supports random pick
'Design a data structure that…' with mixed membership + sampling ops
Anytime O(1) random access is required alongside O(1) membership
antiSignals: No random sampling needed → a plain hash set is enough
Duplicates allowed → RandomizedCollection (LC 381), map value → set of indices
Need ordered iteration / min / max → balanced BST or heap, not this
Need weighted random → prefix-sum + binary search instead of uniform array pick
remember.takeaway: The array+map combo is the canonical 'O(1) everything' design. The swap-with-last delete is the move that makes deletion O(1) without breaking the contiguity that getRandom relies on. Remember to repair the moved element's index — that one line is what separates a working solution from a subtle data-corruption bug.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can compose two simple structures (array + hash map) to hit a complexity that neither achieves alone, and whether you handle the O(1) deletion via swap-with-last correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Deleting from the middle of the array (O(n) shift), or doing the swap but forgetting to update the moved element's index in the map — corrupting future lookups.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY each structure is needed (array → random access & getRandom; map → membership), narrate the swap-with-last carefully including the index repair, and mention the duplicate-allowing follow-up (LC 381).

problemStatement:
Implement the `RandomizedSet` class:

- `RandomizedSet()` initializes the `RandomizedSet` object.
- `bool insert(int val)` inserts an item `val` into the set if not present. Returns `true` if the item was not present, `false` otherwise.
- `bool remove(int val)` removes an item `val` from the set if present. Returns `true` if the item was present, `false` otherwise.
- `int getRandom()` returns a random element from the current set of elements (it's guaranteed that at least one element exists when this method is called). ***Each element must have the same probability of being returned.***

You must implement the functions of the class such that each function works in ***average O(1) time complexity***.
constraints: At most 2 × 10⁵ calls will be made to insert, remove, and getRandom
There will be at least one element in the data structure when getRandom is called
understanding: We need a container with set semantics (no duplicates, O(1) insert/remove/membership) that ALSO supports uniformly random element access in O(1). A hash set alone can't do getRandom in O(1) (you'd have to materialize its elements). An array alone can't do remove in O(1) (deleting a middle element shifts the rest). The trick is to use both and make deletion O(1) by moving the last element into the freed slot.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same value be inserted twice?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — it's a set. insert returns false if the value is already present. The duplicate-allowing variant is RandomizedCollection (LC 381) and needs a map from value to a set of indices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does getRandom need to be exactly uniform?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, every present element must have equal probability. Picking a uniform random index into a contiguous array achieves that directly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(1) required worst-case or average?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Average — hash map operations are O(1) amortized/average, and the array append/pop are amortized O(1). That's acceptable per the spec.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can getRandom be called on an empty structure?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, the constraints guarantee at least one element exists when getRandom is called, so I don't need to guard for an empty array there.

examples.input: insert(1), remove(2), insert(2), getRandom(), remove(1), insert(2), getRandom()
examples.output: true, false, true, [1 or 2], true, false, 2
examples.explanation: insert(1)→true (new). remove(2)→false (absent). insert(2)→true. getRandom→1 or 2 equally. remove(1)→true. insert(2)→false (already present). getRandom→2 (only element).

examples.input: insert(0), insert(1), remove(0), insert(2), remove(1), getRandom()
examples.explanation: After the operations only 2 remains, so getRandom always returns 2. The removes exercise the swap-with-last on both a middle and a tail element.

approaches.name: Single structure (why neither array nor set alone works)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to frame the problem — it shows you understand WHY the combined structure is necessary.
hints: A hash set does insert, remove, and contains in O(1) — but how would you pick a uniformly random element from it in O(1)? You can't index into a set.
A dynamic array makes getRandom trivial (random index) and append O(1) — but removing a value requires finding it (O(n)) and shifting everything after it (O(n)).
Each structure nails two of the three operations and fails the third. The fix is to use both and cover each other's weakness.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Set: getRandom needs to enumerate or copy elements → O(n). Array: remove needs a linear search plus a shift → O(n). Neither hits O(1) on all three.
approaches.explanation:
Before reaching for the combined structure, it's worth seeing exactly why the two obvious single-structure attempts fall short — interviewers reward this framing.

**A hash set alone.** `HashSet` gives `O(1)` average `insert`, `remove`, and `contains`. The wall is `getRandom`: a set has no notion of position, so to pick a uniformly random element you'd have to iterate to a random offset or copy all elements into an array first — both `O(n)`. There is no `O(1)` way to address the k-th element of a hash set.

**A dynamic array alone.** An `ArrayList`/list makes `getRandom` a one-liner (`arr[random index]`) and `insert` an `O(1)` amortized append. The wall here is `remove(val)`: you must first *find* `val` (a linear scan, `O(n)`, since the array isn't sorted or indexed by value) and then *delete* it from the middle, which shifts every later element left — another `O(n)`. Even if you knew the index for free, the shift alone is `O(n)`.

**The lesson.** Each structure is strong exactly where the other is weak: the array provides positional/random access, the set/map provides value-keyed lookup. The optimal design simply runs both in parallel and keeps them in sync — the array stores the elements contiguously for `getRandom`, and a hash map stores `value → index` so we can locate any value in `O(1)` for removal. The only non-trivial part is keeping deletion `O(1)`, which the next approach solves with the swap-with-last trick.
approaches.insight: When no single data structure hits the target complexity on every operation, compose two that are individually strong on disjoint operations and keep them synchronized. 'Array for order/random access + map for value lookup' is one of the most reused composition patterns in design problems.

pitfalls: Believing a HashSet alone satisfies the spec — getRandom is O(n).
Believing an ArrayList alone satisfies it — remove(val) is O(n) (search + shift).
Trying to keep the array sorted for binary search — then insert/remove become O(n) shifts.

approaches.name: Dynamic Array + value→index Hash Map (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer. Walk through insert, then the swap-with-last remove slowly, then getRandom.
hints: Store the elements in a growable array so getRandom is just arr[randomIndex]. Store a map value→index alongside it so you can find any value's position in O(1).
insert: if already in the map return false; else append to the array and record idx[val] = lastIndex.

remove: look up the index i; instead of deleting in place, copy the LAST array element into slot i, update its index in the map, then pop the last slot and erase val from the map. That turns an O(n) shift into O(1).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Map operations and array append/pop/index are all O(1) average. The swap-with-last replaces the O(n) middle-deletion shift with a constant number of operations → O(1) per call. Space is O(n) for the array plus O(n) for the map.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain two structures kept perfectly in sync: a dynamic array `arr` holding the current elements in arbitrary order, and a hash map `idx` mapping each value to **its current index in `arr`**. The array is what makes `getRandom` `O(1)`; the map is what makes membership and locating-for-removal `O(1)`.

**insert.** If `val` is already a key in `idx`, return false — sets reject duplicates. Otherwise append `val` to the end of `arr` and record `idx[val] = arr.size() − 1`. Appending is amortized `O(1)` and the map write is `O(1)`. Done.

**remove — the heart of the problem.** Naively removing `val` from the middle of `arr` would shift every later element, costing `O(n)`. The trick: we don't care about the *order* of elements (getRandom is uniform regardless), so we can fill the hole left by `val` with the **last** element instead of shifting. Concretely: let `i = idx[val]` and `last = arr[arr.size()−1]`. Write `arr[i] = last` (the last element now occupies the victim's slot), update `idx[last] = i` (**critical** — the moved element lives at a new index now), then pop the final slot of `arr` and delete `val` from `idx`. Four `O(1)` operations replace the `O(n)` shift. The single line most candidates forget is `idx[last] = i`: skip it and the map points the moved element at a stale index, silently corrupting later removes and lookups.

**Why swap-with-last is always safe.** Even when `val` *is* the last element, the logic still holds: `last == val`, we write `arr[i] = val` (a no-op), set `idx[val] = i` (a no-op), then pop and delete `val`. No special case needed. And because every element of `arr` is a genuine current member (we never leave tombstones), `getRandom` over `arr`'s indices is exactly uniform over the set.

**getRandom.** The array is contiguous and every slot holds a distinct present element, so `arr[random index in 0..size−1]` returns each element with probability `1/size` — true uniformity in `O(1)`. No copying, no iteration.

**Why the map stores value→index and not the reverse.** The questions we must answer in `O(1)` are *"is `val` present?"* and *"where is `val` so I can remove it?"* — both keyed by value. Indexing by value as the key gives `O(1)` for both. The array already provides the index→value direction for `getRandom`.
approaches.insight: Order doesn't matter, so deletion can cheat: drop the last element into the gap rather than shifting. This 'swap-with-last + pop' is a reusable `O(1)` removal technique for any unordered array-backed collection — the same move appears in heap sift-down setup, RandomizedCollection, and graph adjacency compaction.

edgeCases.input: remove(val) where val is the last element
edgeCases.behavior: last == val: arr[i]=val (no-op), idx[val]=i (no-op), pop, del — works without a special case.

edgeCases.input: insert then remove then insert the same value
edgeCases.behavior: Membership check makes the second insert succeed only after removal; indices stay consistent.
idx.get returns null / 'not in idx' → return false, no mutation.

pitfalls: Forgetting idx[last] = i after the swap — the moved element's index goes stale, corrupting later operations.
Deleting from the middle of the array instead of swapping with the last — O(n) shift.
Updating the map before the array (or vice versa) inconsistently, leaving them out of sync.
Using arr.remove(Integer.valueOf(x)) in Java by value (O(n) search) instead of removing the last index.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to update the moved element's index in the map after swap-with-last.
Removing from the middle of the array (O(n) shift) instead of swapping with the last element.
Using only a hash set (getRandom O(n)) or only an array (remove O(n)).
In Java, calling list.remove(Object) which searches by value — use list.remove(lastIndex).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not repairing the moved element's index
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After moving the last element into the victim's slot, its position changed. If you don't update idx[last], a later remove(last) reads a stale index and corrupts the array.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
i = self.idx[val]
last = self.arr[-1]
self.arr[i] = last
# forgot: self.idx[last] = i
self.arr.pop()
del self.idx[val]
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
i = self.idx[val]
last = self.arr[-1]
self.arr[i] = last
self.idx[last] = i
self.arr.pop()
del self.idx[val]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Deleting from the middle of the array
commonMistakesDetailed.why: list.remove(i) on a middle index shifts every later element, making remove O(n) and breaking the O(1) contract.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Java list.remove(Object) vs remove(index)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: arr.remove(Integer.valueOf(val)) searches the list by value (O(n)) and removes the first match. We want to pop the last index, which is remove(int index).

followupVariations.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) — Duplicates allowed
followupVariations.hint: Map value → SET of indices. On remove, swap any one occurrence with the last and fix both index sets.

followupVariations.title: LRU Cache
followupVariations.hint: Another compose-two-structures design: hash map + doubly linked list for O(1) get/put.

followupVariations.title: LFU Cache
followupVariations.hint: Hash maps plus frequency buckets — same 'combine structures for O(1)' philosophy, harder bookkeeping.

followupVariations.title: Random Pick with Weight
followupVariations.hint: When sampling must be weighted, not uniform — prefix sums + binary search instead of an array index.

patternNote: Compose a dynamic array (positional/random access) with a value→index hash map (O(1) lookup), and use swap-with-last to keep deletion O(1). Recognise it whenever a design problem demands O(1) on a mix of membership and random-sampling operations. The same composition powers RandomizedCollection and is cousin to LRU Cache's map+list design.
